docs.title: RemoteMedia
docs.text:
RemoteMedia runs pipelines of nodes that process audio, video, text, and structured data. Use it to embed media processing in an application, connect models and tools, serve interactive sessions, or distribute work across runners.

Start with the capability map to choose an application, or go directly to the Python API.

docs.title: Choose how to integrate
docs.text: Your goal Start here Execute a pipeline inside a Python application Run locally with FFI Send and receive data over a long-lived local session Stream inputs and outputs Observe or control a distributed session from Python Connect to Scaling Inject context, inspect output, or call a node method Session control and RPC Add your own transform or model implementation Write a Python node

docs.title: Understand the pieces
docs.text:
A pipeline describes nodes and their connections. A node implements one processing step. A session is a live execution context. A client supplies input, consumes output, or controls a session. A plugin makes additional node implementations available to a host. Scaling assigns pipeline work to runners and routes distributed sessions.

These choices can be combined: a Python backend can control a Scaling session whose runners execute Python and native plugin nodes. Individual features still depend on the selected transport, runtime build, and installed plugins.

docs.title: What can I build?
docs.text:
Use RemoteMedia as the execution layer for media applications. Combine processing nodes into a graph, choose how the application connects, and place work on the hosts that have the required models and devices.

docs.title: Execution choices
docs.text:
From Through To Python application FFI Local runtime session Python control client gRPC control attach Scaling Entry, which routes to runner sessions Backend Admin HTTP Scaling Entry deployment/session administration Media participant Admission, runner signaling, then WebRTC Runner session Python or native node Host registration/plugin loading Local host or runner

The local host may still run nodes in worker processes. Remote control attaches to an existing session. A media participant's join and transport negotiation are additional steps. Shared graph concepts do not eliminate these lifecycle differences.

docs.title: Choose a first project
docs.text:
Start with a text echo to verify installation and session lifecycle. Then choose one media operation with a known model and sample input. Add streaming, control, and distribution after the single-host path produces the expected result.

Measure latency and throughput on the intended device. Check speech identity or visual quality with the output itself. Buffer ownership reports, successful execution, and perceptual quality answer different questions.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: Use Python to drive a RemoteMedia pipeline or to implement a node inside one. For local execution, the client calls the native runtime through FFI. For remote operation, the control client attaches to a running session, including a session routed through Scaling Entry.

docs.title: Choose your role
docs.text:
Role Public entry point Runs where? Execute one local request remotemedia.execute_pipeline_with_input(...) Native host in your application process; nodes may use workers Keep a local stream open remotemedia.runtime.create_streaming_session(...) Local runtime session Control an existing local session remotemedia.control.attach_inproc(session) In-process control attach Control an existing remote session remotemedia.control.attach(address, session_id=...) gRPC service or Scaling Entry admin listener Add processing behavior MultiprocessNode, NodeConfig, RuntimeData Host-managed Python worker Compose lightweight Python objects Pipeline, Node Python execution or native instance path, depending on the call

“Python node” means a processing component written in Python; it does not refer to Node.js.

docs.title: Run locally
docs.text:
After installing the client and native runtime, a single-node manifest can echo text:

import asyncio
from remotemedia import execute_pipeline_with_input

manifest = {
    "version": "v1",
    "metadata": {"name": "hello"},
    "nodes": [{"id": "echo", "node_type": "PassThrough"}],
    "connections": [],
}

async def main():
    result = await execute_pipeline_with_input(manifest, ["hello"])
    print(result)

asyncio.run(main())

This explicitly requires FFI. The general Pipeline.run() convenience method can fall back to Python after native availability or execution failures; it is a different choice when execution identity matters.

docs.title: Stream, control, and extend
docs.text:
• Streaming: send repeated inputs, consume all output kinds, finish input, and close.
  • Scaling: attach through Entry, and understand deployment, joins, and media transport.
  • Control and RPC: tap outputs, inject context, change node state, and call exposed methods.
  • Python nodes: transform RuntimeData with explicit configuration and lifecycle hooks.
  • Data and buffers: use typed payloads and understand copy ownership.
  • Shared sessions: attribute participant output and distinguish model reuse.
  • Cancellation: interrupt or abort a real generator.
  • Source plugins: package and provision a Python node.
  • RPC and tools: host application callbacks locally or through Entry.
  • Python WebRTC: negotiate a room and exchange audio.
  • Observability: inspect performance and copy reports.
  • API map: find the public surface for each task.

A local FFI session and a remote attach have different creation and ownership contracts. Use separate setup examples even when later control operations share an API.

docs.title: Interrupt or abort generation
docs.text: A generating node must cooperate with cancellation. Declare its modality with a generator mixin such as TextGenerator or AudioGenerator, choose its cancellation strategy, check the active call's token, and implement the state cleanup required by its disposition.

docs.title: Choose the disposition
docs.text:
Disposition Partial output/state Pending input Disposition.INTERRUPT Retain Retain Disposition.ABORT Discard Discard

The disposition describes the generator's contract. It does not retract bytes already received by a client or sound already played by a device. Do not equate cancelling a local asyncio task with completing this runtime contract.

docs.title: Run the text and audio checks
docs.text:
Use the MS2 native profile:

python examples/python/generation_cancel.py
python examples/python/audio_cancel.py

Keep generator_node.py, node_transform.py, and worker_session.py alongside the launchers.

The deterministic text generator declares CancelStrategy.OBSERVES_TOKEN. Each call captures self.cancel_token, checks it between chunks, and yields every 20 ms. Its cancel(call, cancellation) hook commits the partial turn only for retain semantics. It exposes generation_state() to verify which hook ran and what history remains.

The text check first runs assert_generator_cancels_async(..., stateful=True) against the in-memory worker-loop harness. It then repeats interrupt and abort in real host-managed workers, verifies the disposition, checks that no output arrives after the 250 ms test allowance, and proves that the next call sees the expected history. In-memory conformance alone would not establish Rust-host behavior.

For an already attached control client, this excerpt injects a barge-in carrying the intended disposition:

from remotemedia.control import Data
from remotemedia.core.cancel import Disposition

async def interrupt(ctrl):
    await ctrl.publish("worker.in.barge_in", Data.from_json({
        "disposition": Disposition.INTERRUPT.to_dict(),
    }))

The audio check generates 24 kHz mono float32 chunks of 480 samples, cancels after the first chunk, and observes the FFI receiver for 350 ms. It asserts zero samples received later than 250 ms after the cancellation request. This is a bounded synthetic transport check, not a maximum-latency guarantee, a speaker playback test, or a listening evaluation.

docs.title: Keep cancellation responsive
docs.text:
The example yields to the event loop between chunks. Long blocking model work cannot observe the token while it owns the thread; use a model's supported stopping mechanism or a suitable execution strategy. Preserve upstream model controls and document what cannot be interrupted.

Use separate mechanisms for a reply deadline, stopping generation, closing an attach, and closing a session. The examples drain their next text call before session close and stop receiver tasks explicitly. The current Windows native profile can still log a copy-accounting shutdown error; the retained limitation is not evidence that cancellation failed or that accounting closed successfully.

docs.title: Control sessions and call RPC
docs.text: A control attach lets application code interact with named nodes in a running session. Use it for transcript taps, context injection, debugging, node state changes, and exposed RPC methods.

docs.title: Attach locally or remotely
docs.text:
Use attach_inproc(session) with an FFI streaming session, or attach(address, session_id=...) with a compatible gRPC service. For Scaling, follow the Entry setup requirements.

Run the self-contained local example after installation:

python examples/python/control_echo.py

The example creates an echo session, subscribes, publishes hello, and prints the tapped text. It closes the iterator, attach, and session. The main operation is:

import asyncio
from remotemedia.control import attach_inproc

async def tap_echo(session):
    async with attach_inproc(session) as ctrl:
        tap = await ctrl.subscribe("echo.out")
        try:
            await ctrl.publish("echo.in", "hello")
            item = await asyncio.wait_for(anext(tap), timeout=5)
            print(item.text)
        finally:
            await tap.aclose()

subscribe() is awaited to obtain an async iterator. Subscribe before publishing if you need to observe that publication. These are live taps, not a history query.

docs.text:
The table below describes the reviewed checkout. The tested release client supports the local subscribe/publish example; input taps, output publication, metadata keywords, and endpoint hosting require newer checkout APIs. Check availability before using them in a release environment.

Task API Meaning Observe a node's output await ctrl.subscribe("node.out") Returns an async iterator of Data Observe a node's input await ctrl.subscribe_in("node.in") Input-side tap Inject input await ctrl.publish("node.in", data) Accepts a Data wrapper or text string Inject attributed input ctrl.publish(..., metadata=...) Accepts metadata; see the tested input-tap limitation Publish to output subscribers await ctrl.publish_out("node.out", data) Control-bus delivery to output taps; does not enqueue downstream graph execution Inspect/edit/drop output ctrl.intercept(...) Interception has a deadline and decision contract Change processing state ctrl.set_node_state(...), ctrl.clear_node_state(...) Explicit state override and reset Expose application callbacks ctrl.host_endpoint(...) Application-owned endpoint lifecycle

Named ports extend the address, for example llm.in.context. The target graph must expose the corresponding node/port. Unknown nodes, invalid address directions, missing sessions, and remote authorization failures are separate error conditions.

docs.title: Call a node method
docs.text:
Worker nodes can expose methods with remotemedia.rpc.rpc. @rpc(reply=True) declares a result-bearing method; streamed and fire-and-forget modes have different contracts. An attached client resolves node proxies through ctrl.<node_id>.

For a node named formatter that actually exposes a reply method named describe, an application excerpt is:

async def describe_formatter(ctrl):
    return await ctrl.formatter.describe()

This is illustrative, not a method supplied by PassThrough. The node example exposes its own describe() method and exercises it through a real worker in the checkout environment. That check confirms the configured prefix and a process ID different from the host. RPC results follow the RPC reply protocol and should not be treated as ordinary media output.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text: Use session control for downstream intercept effects and node-state checks, and RPC and application tools for complete worker RPC and endpoint examples.

docs.title: Own the lifecycle
docs.text:
The control context closes its transport and proxies; closing the attach does not close the pipeline. Close tap/stream iterators when exiting early. Handle timeouts and cancellation at the call boundary, and keep slow consumer work off a high-volume observation path.

Transport capabilities differ. For example, endpoints() exposes richer details in-process than over gRPC. Use per-operation reference pages before assuming equivalent behavior across a local session and Scaling.

docs.title: Send data and manage buffers
docs.text: A streaming session accepts text and typed runtime dictionaries. remotemedia.control.Data builds several of those dictionaries; a worker receives the separate RuntimeData type. Convert at the boundary with Data.as_runtime_data() when calling native send_input().

docs.title: Run the round trips
docs.text:
Use the MS2 native profile, then run:

python examples/python/data_buffers.py

The complete example checks eight payload kinds through a native PassThrough session and retains an audio view after closing it. This is data transport validation; it does not decode a file or display an image.

Kind Input used by the example Output contract checked Text Python str Text in the data output queue JSON Data.from_json({...}) Dictionary with type: json and value Binary Data.from_buffer(bytes) Buffer export with unchanged bytes Audio Contiguous NumPy float32, 24,000 Hz, one channel Samples, rate, channels; read-only memoryview Tensor Raw float32 bytes, shape [2, 3], runtime dtype code 0 Byte contents, shape and dtype preserved Video Packed 2 × 2 Rgb24, codec=None Pixel bytes and dimensions Image Raw format with pixel_format: Rgb24 Pixel bytes and dimensions File Path, filename, MIME type Reference metadata; no file read or upload

Tensor dtype codes belong to the runtime wire type, not NumPy's numeric dtype IDs. Audio channel layout, video pixel layout, shape and byte length must agree. The example's one-dimensional audio is mono; do not relabel a stereo buffer as mono or change only its sample-rate metadata to resample it.

docs.title: Keep the owner alive
docs.text:
This excerpt creates an audio wrapper without first converting its samples to a list:

import numpy as np
from remotemedia.control import Data

samples = np.zeros(480, dtype=np.float32)
audio = Data.from_audio_numpy(samples, sample_rate=24000, channels=1)
payload = audio.as_runtime_data()
assert payload["samples"] is samples

That identity check describes the Python wrapper. It does not prove that the native host, IPC transport, downstream node, codec, or device makes no copies. Keep input owners alive and do not mutate them while the runtime may still borrow them.

In the tested native profile, audio output is an owning read-only memoryview. np.asarray(value["samples"]) exposes a read-only view; the returned owner keeps the data valid after session close. Use np.array(view, copy=True) when you need a detached writable array. tensor.tobytes() in the example is also an intentional copy.

docs.title: Request and inspect a copy policy
docs.text:
await session.send_input(payload, require_zero_copy=True) applies a strict policy at that input operation. A Python list of audio samples requires materialization: the example deliberately receives BufferError and checks the copy report. A strict input request is not a promise of zero copies throughout an arbitrary graph.

PipelineBufferConfig(policy=...) provides session-level policy and retention limits in builds that expose it. Preflight and node support can reject a graph or operation. Use the copy and performance reports to identify the boundary and reason; do not infer zero-copy support from an accepted NumPy array alone.

docs.text: Choose local execution when Python should own a native runtime, or remote control when the runtime already runs on Scaling. Use separate environments: the published client and current checkout have different APIs despite both reporting version 0.2.0.

docs.text:

A supplied Windows wheel is required

docs.title: Local execution
docs.text:
Run these PowerShell commands from the documentation repository. They assume uv and CPython 3.12.3 are installed. Replace the wheel path with your supplied artifact.

uv venv --python 3.12.3 .venv-runtime
$wheel = "C:\path\to\remotemedia_ffi-0.4.4-cp310-abi3-win_amd64.whl"
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath $wheel
uv pip install --python .venv-runtime/Scripts/python.exe -r examples/python/requirements-local.txt $wheel
.venv-runtime/Scripts/python.exe examples/python/doctor.py --require-ffi
.venv-runtime/Scripts/python.exe examples/python/ffi_echo.py

Expected final output: hello. The diagnostic prints the imported client path, native path, and versions. Optional model-import warnings can appear; these text examples do not require those models.

The tested wheel SHA-256 is:

28c33e00174973c3a3421426207066ab0487d364f51ba61d0f502d456f771426

Its distribution version is 0.4.4; get_runtime_version() reports native runtime 0.4.1. Its build commit is unverified. The artifact filename's ABI tag and the current checkout's Python minimum are different metadata; neither expands the tested matrix above.

The local requirements pin the client and its resolved dependencies. psutil is included only for the process-cleanup checks.

docs.title: Authenticated Scaling control
docs.text:
Place this repository beside remotemedia-sdk. Install the checkout client, which supplies the token= parameter missing from the published client:

uv venv --python 3.12.3 .venv-control
uv pip install --python .venv-control/Scripts/python.exe -r examples/scaling/requirements.txt -e ../remotemedia-sdk/clients/python
.venv-control/Scripts/python.exe examples/python/doctor.py

The Scaling requirements pin dependencies used for this run, including the authentication harness. No native FFI package is needed in this environment. Proceed to Connect to Scaling for the Entry/runner example.

A version string alone cannot distinguish these clients. The reviewed checkout's attach() includes token and participant; see API reference. Do not overlay that checkout onto the local wheel environment without validating native/worker compatibility.

docs.text:
Use the checkout client and its matching native build for the worker walkthrough. The published client cannot discover this example's dotted class path. The checkout must also include the RPC reply-reader fix that removes the worker's rpc text-channel header before parsing JSON; the reviewed file hash is recorded in sources.json.

uv venv --python 3.12.3 .venv-worker
$workerWheel = "C:\path\to\remotemedia_ffi-0.4.4-cp311-abi3-win_amd64.whl"
uv pip install --python .venv-worker/Scripts/python.exe -r examples/python/requirements-worker.txt ../remotemedia-sdk/clients/python $workerWheel

.venv-worker/Scripts/python.exe scripts/verify_examples.py --worker

Install the client normally, as shown, so it and the native extension share the same package directory. The worker requirements pin the tested dependencies. On Windows, the host and worker also need write access to the iceoryx2 paths under C:\Temp; see IPC troubleshooting.

The tested worker wheel SHA-256 is 735300c727f2c72d3c26b4ff022e36ad6fa0dcaf8e4e6de6776c54dca5cccb55. It was built with Maturin 1.16.0, the dev profile, default FFI features disabled, and extension-module enabled (which also enables python). The native module reports 0.4.1. This repository retains the source/build fingerprints in its planning evidence; the wheel itself is a local artifact, not a published download.

Continue with local FFI, Scaling control, or node authoring.

docs.title: Advanced Python (MS2) profile
docs.text:
The advanced guides use a separate Windows x64 / CPython 3.12.3 environment and the captured checkout client with the RPC reply-header fix. Use the worker dependency pins and an MS2 native wheel built with extension-module,grpc,remotemedia-core/python-source-plugin. The earlier MS1 wheel has neither gRPC serving nor source-plugin loading enabled.

uv venv --python 3.12.3 .venv-ms2
$ms2Wheel = "C:/path/to/ms2/remotemedia_ffi-0.4.4-cp311-abi3-win_amd64.whl"
uv pip install --python .venv-ms2/Scripts/python.exe -r examples/python/requirements-worker.txt ../remotemedia-sdk/clients/python $ms2Wheel

.venv-ms2/Scripts/python.exe scripts/verify_examples.py --milestone2

Build the wheel with Maturin 1.16.0 from a compatible SDK/base/plugin-SDK workspace. The validation build used --profile dev --no-default-features --features extension-module,grpc,remotemedia-core/python-source-plugin. Its artifact hashes and captured source identity are retained in the repository's MS2 validation record. The distribution is still 0.4.4 and the native runtime reports 0.4.1; distinguish builds by features and hashes, not those version strings alone. This repository does not distribute the wheel.

The source-plugin gate uses uv on PATH to provision its environment and install packaging==25.0. It has a 150-second outer deadline. Other examples have a 65-second process deadline. The verifier records functional results, descendant cleanup, and copy-accounting shutdown errors separately.

docs.text:

docs.title: Run a pipeline locally with FFI
docs.text: Call execute_pipeline_with_input() to execute a manifest through the native runtime. This is useful when your application owns the input and needs the result of one request.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: Install the client and compatible native runtime. The example uses the built-in PassThrough node and needs no model download or GPU.

docs.title: Execute a request
docs.text:
From the documentation repository root:

python examples/python/ffi_echo.py

The complete example loads echo.json. Run it with the local environment's Python, or activate that environment first. Its source is included directly here:

"""Execute one request through the native FFI. Requires client + native runtime."""

import asyncio
import json
from pathlib import Path

from remotemedia import execute_pipeline_with_input


async def main():
    manifest = json.loads(Path(__file__).with_name("echo.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    result = await asyncio.wait_for(
        execute_pipeline_with_input(manifest, ["hello"]), timeout=10
    )
    assert result == "hello", result
    print(result)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Expected output is the string hello. The script asserts that result and applies a ten-second application timeout. This return shape was verified with the local FFI profile; other graphs and metrics-enabled calls can return different envelopes.

docs.title: Choose the execution contract
docs.text:
Entry point Behavior to account for execute_pipeline_with_input(manifest, [item]) Explicit native path; missing FFI raises an import error execute_pipeline(...) Native execution without caller-supplied input, for an appropriate source-driven graph Pipeline.run(input_data, use_rust=True) Attempts native execution and can fall back to Python, including after execution errors Pipeline.run(..., use_rust=False) Chooses the Python executor

The reviewed wrapper documents manifest execution as validating the input list but executing only its first item. Use one input here. Use a streaming session for repeated requests. Direct Node instance lists follow a different path; their behavior should not be inferred from manifest execution.

docs.title: Errors and lifecycle
docs.text:
The one-shot call owns its execution; it does not return a long-lived session to close. A timeout limits the application's wait, not proof that all native or worker work has already terminated. Invalid manifests, unknown node types, and missing plugin dependencies must be resolved before execution succeeds.

For long-running work, use a session with an explicit close() in finally. Continue with streaming.

docs.title: Implement a transform
docs.text:
The complete example registers DocsUppercase, reads a prefix from NodeConfig.params, uppercases text, and exposes an RPC description method:

"""Direct worker-node contract check; does not launch a host or worker process."""

import asyncio
import os

from remotemedia.core.multiprocessing import MultiprocessNode, NodeConfig, register_node
from remotemedia.core.multiprocessing.data import RuntimeData
from remotemedia.rpc import rpc


@register_node("DocsUppercase")
class DocsUppercase(MultiprocessNode):
    def __init__(self, config: NodeConfig):
        if not isinstance(config, NodeConfig):
            raise TypeError("DocsUppercase requires NodeConfig with manifest parameters")
        super().__init__(config)
        self.prefix = str(config.params.get("prefix", ""))

    async def initialize(self):
        # Load model or device resources here when your node needs them.
        pass

    async def process(self, data: RuntimeData) -> RuntimeData:
        if not data.is_text():
            raise TypeError("DocsUppercase expects text input")
        return RuntimeData.text(self.prefix + data.as_text().upper())

    @rpc(reply=True)
    async def describe(self) -> dict:
        return {"operation": "uppercase", "prefix": self.prefix, "pid": os.getpid()}

    async def cleanup(self):
        # Release any resources allocated during initialize().
        pass


async def main():
    try:
        DocsUppercase("formatter")
    except TypeError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError("A bare node ID must not discard manifest parameters")
    node = DocsUppercase(NodeConfig("formatter", "DocsUppercase", {"prefix": "DOCS: "}))
    try:
        await node.initialize()
        output = await node.process(RuntimeData.text("hello"))
        print(output.as_text())
        assert output.as_text() == "DOCS: HELLO"
        assert await node.describe() == {"operation": "uppercase", "prefix": "DOCS: ", "pid": os.getpid()}
    finally:
        await node.cleanup()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

The host constructs a node with NodeConfig(node_id, node_type, params, session_id, ...). Parameters must reach the constructor; the example explicitly raises TypeError on a bare node ID so a legacy construction fallback cannot silently discard manifest configuration. initialize() loads resources, process() handles each input, and cleanup() releases resources.

Run the direct contract check:

python examples/python/node_transform.py

Expected output: DOCS: HELLO. This directly exercises configuration and node methods. It does not launch a worker or validate plugin discovery, IPC, or process teardown.

docs.title: Execute in a worker
docs.text:
First install the worker environment. The worker harness registers the dotted class path with the native host and adds the module directory to the child's import path. Its manifest selects sys.prefix with python_env.explicit_venv, so the worker uses the environment containing the installed client and IPC dependencies.

.venv-worker/Scripts/python.exe scripts/verify_examples.py --worker

The verified result is WORKER: HELLO, an RPC reply containing prefix: "WORKER: ", and a worker PID different from the host PID. The verifier requires the host and observed child processes to terminate normally. The Windows run passed all six checks with no forced cleanup or remaining children. This distinguishes host construction and IPC from the direct class test.

Use the matching client and native build

The passing profile uses the checkout client with the RPC reply-header fix, a matching Python extension, and writable Windows IPC paths. The published client alone does not provide this path. The source-plugin guide validates local loading and managed dependencies. Remote package publication remains a separate release task.

"""Execute DocsUppercase in a real worker using the current environment explicitly."""

import asyncio
import json
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import remotemedia.runtime as rt
from remotemedia.control import attach_inproc


async def main():
    # The worker imports this on-disk module; it does not inherit this process's registry.
    module_dir = str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent)
    os.environ["PYTHONPATH"] = os.pathsep.join(filter(None, [module_dir, os.environ.get("PYTHONPATH")]))
    rt.register_python_node_type("DocsUppercase", python_class="node_transform.DocsUppercase")
    manifest = {
        "version": "v1",
        "metadata": {"name": "docs-worker"},
        "python_env": {"explicit_venv": sys.prefix},
        "nodes": [{"id": "formatter", "node_type": "DocsUppercase", "params": {"prefix": "WORKER: "}}],
        "connections": [],
    }
    session = await asyncio.wait_for(rt.create_streaming_session(json.dumps(manifest)), timeout=45)
    try:
        await session.send_input("hello")
        kind, value = await asyncio.wait_for(session.recv_output(), timeout=10)
        assert (kind, value) == ("data", "WORKER: HELLO"), (kind, value)
        async with attach_inproc(session) as ctrl:
            description = await asyncio.wait_for(ctrl.formatter.describe(), timeout=10)
        assert description["prefix"] == "WORKER: "
        assert description["pid"] != os.getpid(), "The node must execute in a separate process"
        print(json.dumps({"output": value, "worker_pid": description["pid"], "host_pid": os.getpid()}))
    finally:
        await session.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

@register_node("DocsUppercase") registers the class when its module is imported. A host/worker must discover and import that module; decoration alone does not install it on another runner.

A source plugin adds a plugin.toml with the plugin identity, Python entry module, declared node types, module root, and dependencies. The host's source-plugin path also reads the node's __python_version__ parameter when selecting its managed environment. They declare the generated modality and cancellation strategy and implement async cancel(self, call, cancellation). Interrupt and abort have different state/input semantics. Use the SDK's generator conformance helper and a real host test before documenting responsive barge-in or output-tail guarantees.

docs.title: Inspect runtime activity and copies
docs.text: Use runtime observations to explain where a pipeline is spending time and how data crosses instrumented boundaries. Name the scope of a counter before using it to compare implementations.

docs.title: Read a performance snapshot
docs.text:
With the MS2 native profile:

python examples/python/observability.py

The complete example sets REMOTEMEDIA_PERF_TAP=1 before creating the session, subscribes to __perf__.out, sends four text inputs, and waits up to five seconds for a snapshot. The publisher emits on a one-second interval in the reviewed runtime.

Snapshots include session identity, timestamp, window length and per-node data such as input/output counts and latency summaries. The example is a tiny CPU text workload, useful for validating the API. Four messages do not establish a stable latency percentile or real-device performance.

docs.title: Separate copy boundaries
docs.text:
API or field Scope session.input_copy_report() Input materialization/transport authorities, grouped by policy and reason session.node_copy_reports() Instrumented node boundaries and their copy authorities copied_bytes, completed Recorded completed copies at that boundary rejected_bytes, rejected Requests denied by policy; not completed copies failed, in_flight, saturated Incomplete, outstanding, or bounded-accounting conditions that affect interpretation

Do not sum unrelated scopes as if they were a single physical memory counter. A zero value can describe an unexercised path; it does not prove no allocator, codec, Python library, driver or device made a copy. The data example deliberately rejects list materialization under a strict input policy and records the result.

Worker shutdown can leave a copy-accounting closure error in the tested Windows native profile while every process exits. Keep that diagnostic in the evidence. Do not use those shutdown records to claim complete accounting conservation.

docs.title: Events and placement
docs.text:
recv_event() exposes attributed participant output; the shared-session example verifies it. __system__.out is the reviewed lifecycle event tap and __timeline__.out carries diagnostic markers. Those tap contracts are source-reviewed here; this example executes the performance tap. A live subscription is not a persisted event history.

Scaling placement belongs to Entry and the runners' advertised capabilities. The local harness provides one runner with static discovery and records its binary hashes. It does not test placement across multiple machines, failover, or dynamic capacity. Correlate session, node and participant identifiers with the server logs before attributing a delay to placement.

docs.title: Measure the user-facing result separately
docs.text:
For a real audio/video application, retain the physical device, model/artifact identity, representative input, startup time, sustained run duration, latency boundary and output artifact. Use listening or visual evaluation when quality is the acceptance criterion. An API test, a performance snapshot, and a device benchmark answer different questions.

docs.text: This reference covers the calls used by the runnable guides. Release means the tested local FFI environment; checkout means the SDK source client used in the separate Scaling and worker environments. Method signatures below omit self. An await is required for operations marked async, including native methods returning Python awaitables.

Both clients report 0.2.0. Select an environment by its imported files and dependency set, rather than by that version alone.

docs.title: One request through FFI
docs.text:
Import from remotemedia. Exact release call signatures, with annotations omitted:

async execute_pipeline(pipeline_or_manifest, enable_metrics=False) -> Any
async execute_pipeline_with_input(pipeline_or_manifest, input_data, enable_metrics=False) -> Any

The checkout adds keyword-only pipeline_buffers=None to both calls. It accepts a pipeline object, node list, JSON string, or manifest dictionary. The guides use a dictionary and a one-item input list. The reviewed manifest path validates all inputs but executes only the first; use a stream for multiple requests.

For the tested PassThrough graph without metrics, the return value is the echoed string. Metrics-enabled and other graph outputs have different envelopes. These calls own their execution and return no session handle. An application timeout bounds waiting; it does not certify that native work has stopped.

Error Condition ImportError Native module missing or unable to load TypeError input_data is not a list, or unsupported manifest/node-list type ValueError Empty input list, empty pipeline, or invalid manifest RuntimeError Runtime execution or node initialization failure

The empty-list branch raises ValueError even though an older wrapper docstring lists it under TypeError. The lifecycle probe checks the actual behavior. Pipeline.run(use_rust=True) can retry through Python after native errors; it has different execution semantics.

docs.title: Native streaming session
docs.text:
Import remotemedia.runtime as rt. Tested release signatures:

await rt.create_streaming_session(manifest_json) -> PyStreamingSession
await session.send_input(data) -> None
await session.recv_output() -> tuple[str, Any] | None
await session.signal_input_complete() -> None
await session.close() -> None

manifest_json is a JSON string, not a dictionary. Parse errors raise ValueError; executor/session creation failures raise RuntimeError. The caller owns the resulting session and must close it in finally.

send_input() converts supported Python values into runtime data. Strings are text inputs. Data-conversion errors occur before queuing; sending after input completion or close raises RuntimeError. A successful send means the input was queued, not that every downstream node has finished.

recv_output() consumes one output from the shared audio/video/data queues and returns (kind, value). Text echoes are ("data", "hello"). None means all relevant output channels are closed. Use one receiving strategy per session; kind-specific receivers and recv_output() compete for the same queues.

Input completion drops the external input sender. In the tested artifact it does not establish natural EOF for the echo graph. Receive the graph's expected result count or application completion event, stop receiving tasks, then close. Explicit close discards unread output, is idempotent, and makes subsequent receive return None. See the tested lifecycle.

The checkout adds pipeline_buffers=None to creation and require_zero_copy=False to send. These signatures are present in the worker wheel, but absent in the supplied release wheel. The examples use their defaults; copy accounting is not an end-to-end zero-copy guarantee.

docs.title: Attach control
docs.text:
Import attach and attach_inproc from remotemedia.control. Both return async context managers yielding AttachedSession:

# Release
attach(address, *, session_id, attach_id='python-client', credentials=None)
attach_inproc(session)

# Checkout
attach(address, *, session_id, attach_id='python-client', credentials=None,
       token=None, participant=None)

address is host:port. credentials is a gRPC channel-credentials object; None selects plaintext. The checkout sends a bearer token from token, or REMOTEMEDIA_CONTROL_TOKEN when the argument is None. Scaling requires a backend token. participant is a participant ID or metadata mapping for attribution; it is not media admission.

attach_inproc() uses a live FFI session without a network connection. Closing either control context closes its transport and proxies, not the pipeline session. The FFI owner or Scaling administration still owns session teardown.

docs.title: Observe and publish
docs.text:
async ctrl.subscribe(address: str) -> AsyncIterator[Data]
async ctrl.publish(address: str, data: Data | str) -> None
async ctrl.close() -> None

Await subscribe() first, then iterate its result. Subscribe to node.out before publishing to node.in when you need to observe that input's output. Named ports use node.in.port or node.out.port. Close the iterator with await tap.aclose() on early exit.

Data here is remotemedia.control.Data; .text accesses a text payload. Worker RuntimeData is a different type. Publication returning None is not an application-result acknowledgement. Wait for the expected tap output or an RPC reply as appropriate.

The checkout's publish signature additionally accepts keyword-only metadata: Mapping[str, str] | None = None. It also provides subscribe_in(address) for input taps and publish_out(address, data, *, metadata=None) for output control-bus subscribers. Output publication does not enqueue downstream processing. Entry tap traffic is capped and may be dropped; subscription is a live observation channel.

Error surface Meaning ControlAddressError Malformed address or wrong .in/.out direction SessionNotFoundError Attach cannot resolve the live session UnknownNodeError Address references an absent node; may arrive through the event stream gRPC transport/auth errors Unreachable service, rejected credentials/token, closed connection TimeoutError from asyncio.wait_for The application's deadline expired

The protocol uses one bidirectional PipelineControl.Attach stream: a session-identifying Hello, then control frames and events. The Python client handles that framing. Server errors may arrive asynchronously; successful enqueue alone cannot confirm remote processing.

docs.text:
Import MultiprocessNode, NodeConfig, and register_node from remotemedia.core.multiprocessing; import RuntimeData from its data module.

NodeConfig(node_id: str, node_type: str, params: dict,
           session_id: str | None = None, log_level: str = 'INFO')
async node.initialize() -> None
async node.process(data: RuntimeData) -> RuntimeData | AsyncGenerator | None
async node.cleanup() -> None
register_node(node_type: str)
rt.register_python_node_type(node_type, python_class=None, multi_output=False,
                             description=None, category=None, accepts=None, produces=None)

The host supplies configuration, calls initialization before processing, and owns cleanup. @register_node registers a class when its Python module is imported; native register_python_node_type tells the host the importable dotted class path. Both sides must resolve the same type. In the example, RuntimeData.text(...), .is_text(), and .as_text() construct/check/read the worker payload; non-text input raises the example's TypeError.

The direct class test validates parameter use and method behavior. The real worker check also validates configuration transport, transformed output, RPC with a distinct process ID, and normal termination of observed children.

docs.title: Reply RPC
docs.text:
rpc(func=None, *, reply=False, stream=False, timeout=None)

Import the decorator from remotemedia.rpc. The node example marks describe() with @rpc(reply=True). The client calls await ctrl.formatter.describe(); method names and arguments are supplied by the actual node, not by PassThrough. Reply-mode failures use RpcError; a reply deadline uses RpcTimeoutError. RPC replies travel over their own correlated protocol and are distinct from media outputs. See the executed RPC and endpoint examples and generation cancellation checks for transport-specific behavior and limits.

docs.title: Connect to Scaling from Python
docs.text: Use remotemedia.control.attach() to control a live distributed session through Scaling Entry. Entry resolves node addresses to runner partitions and forwards control operations. Python uses the same control attach surface as a compatible standalone gRPC host.

docs.title: Before you attach
docs.text:
Use the checkout control environment. The published 0.2.0 client lacks token= and cannot run this authenticated example unchanged.

You need a running Entry deployment, its admin gRPC address, a backend token when authentication is enabled, and an existing session. The session can be addressed by its internal ID or by <pipeline>/<session key>.

Attaching does not deploy a pipeline, join a media participant, or start a session. A token for a media client is not the backend token required by this admin control interface.

docs.title: Run a complete local control walkthrough
docs.text:
The harness starts an authenticated Entry and one real runner. Supply an existing compatible Scaling build directory containing remotemedia-scaling-entry.exe and remotemedia-scaling-runner.exe:

.venv-control/Scripts/python.exe examples/scaling/run.py --bin-dir C:/path/to/scaling-build

Expected output:

hello through Entry
PASS: authenticated Entry control, runner echo, admission, and teardown. Evidence: .../result.json

The harness chooses free ports, generates an ephemeral Ed25519 key, and signs separate short-lived backend and client tokens. It verifies an unauthenticated admin request returns 401, deploys the echo manifest, admits a client to create the session, subscribes to echo.out, then publishes to echo.in through Entry. Deployment's path name must match metadata.name in the manifest.

Tokens are not printed. The private key stays in memory; the public key, server logs, and binary hashes go in .run/scaling/<run>/. The harness deletes its session and pipeline, then stops and reaps only the servers it started. This plaintext setup is for local evaluation; existing deployments should supply appropriate channel credentials.

The check covers control routing through Entry to a runner and client admission. It does not establish WebRTC media negotiation, multi-runner placement, failover, or model performance. Server binary commits are unverified; their hashes are recorded in the validation report.

docs.title: Observe a node
docs.text:
The complete remote control example reads REMOTEMEDIA_CONTROL_ADDRESS, REMOTEMEDIA_SESSION_ID, and optionally REMOTEMEDIA_CONTROL_TOKEN. REMOTEMEDIA_TAP selects an output address and defaults to echo.out. Set these for your existing deployment, then run:

python examples/python/remote_control.py

It waits up to 30 seconds for one new tapped output and then detaches. Produce input through the running application after the subscription opens. No output within that window raises a timeout; it does not establish that the session is broken.

The core operation is:

from remotemedia.control import attach

async def observe(address, session_id, token):
    async with attach(address, session_id=session_id, token=token) as ctrl:
        tap = await ctrl.subscribe("echo.out")
        try:
            async for item in tap:
                print(item.text)
        finally:
            await tap.aclose()

Use host:port for the gRPC address, not an HTTP URL. attach() accepts gRPC channel credentials for a secured deployment. The complete example targets a local/private plaintext admin listener; adapt transport credentials to your deployment.

docs.title: Separate deployment, admission, and control
docs.text:
Operation Interface Who uses it? Deploy or replace a named pipeline Admin HTTP PUT /pipelines/{name} with {"manifest": ..., "warm": 0} Backend Join a session Public HTTP POST /join or Entry signaling Client with a token identifying pipeline/session/member Connect participant media Runner signal_url, admission ticket, then WebRTC negotiation Media client Tap/publish/intercept/call node RPC Admin gRPC PipelineControl through Python attach() Backend Inspect placement Admin HTTP /sessions/{id}/placement and event stream Operator/backend

The join response supplies runner signaling information and a ticket; it is not itself a media stream. Clients do not submit manifests in joins. Continue with the executed Python WebRTC guide for negotiation, audio delivery and cleanup. The example composes HTTP, control and media APIs; no dedicated ScalingClient facade is assumed.

docs.title: Lifecycle and limits
docs.text:
Leaving async with attach(...) closes that control attach. It does not end the distributed session. Session/member termination uses separate administration operations.

Entry caps relayed tap traffic per attach; the reviewed default is 1 MiB/s, with excess tap frames dropped and counted. Taps support observation and do not promise lossless media delivery or replay. Node movement, runner loss, and recovery depend on placement/state-class rules; reconnecting a control client is not arbitrary checkpoint restoration.

Continue with control and RPC for shared operations and the API map for their entry points.

docs.title: Call methods and host application tools
docs.text: Use RPC to call a method exposed by a worker node. Use an application endpoint when the node needs to ask your application for a tool result, policy decision, or external service response. Both have correlated replies; a media output tap is a separate channel.

docs.title: Exercise worker RPC modes
docs.text:
Install the MS2 native profile. Keep advanced_nodes.py, node_transform.py, and worker_session.py beside the client example:

python examples/python/rpc_modes.py

The complete client verifies a separate worker PID, configuration, streamed replies, fire-and-forget state changes, remote errors, and a deadline.

Worker declaration Client use Result @rpc(reply=True) await ctrl.worker.describe() One correlated value @rpc(stream=True) async for value in ctrl.worker.words(...) Stream of correlated values @rpc await ctrl.worker.configure(...) Fire-and-forget dispatch; no application-result reply

When leaving a stream early, close the iterator returned by aiter(call). The deferred call object itself has no aclose():

async def first_word(ctrl):
    stream = aiter(ctrl.worker.words("one two three"))
    try:
        return await anext(stream)
    finally:
        await stream.aclose()

Use _timeout=... for a reply deadline. Remote method failures raise RpcError; a local reply deadline raises RpcTimeoutError. A deadline ending your wait does not establish that remote work stopped. Use the node's cancellation contract when work must stop. The example confirms that a later call still succeeds after a timed-out call.

docs.title: Let a worker call your application
docs.text:
Run either transport against a real worker:

python examples/python/application_endpoint.py
python examples/python/application_endpoint_grpc.py

The worker calls await self.call_endpoint("application", "decorate", text=..., deadline_ms=3000) inside process(). The application hosts that name, receives an EndpointCall, checks the method and arguments, replies, and observes APP: HELLO as the processed output. The gRPC launcher runs the same flow through a loopback GrpcServer; it requires the native grpc feature.

For an already attached ctrl, the essential registration is:

async def serve_one(ctrl):
    host = await ctrl.host_endpoint("application", methods={"decorate": "reply"})
    try:
        call = await anext(host)
        ack = await call.reply({"text": call.kwargs["text"].upper()})
        assert ack.accepted
    finally:
        await host.close()

Production code should bound the wait, validate arguments, and handle endpoint errors. Hosting belongs to an attach, not to the lifetime of the model. Closing the host unregisters it; gRPC unregistration is asynchronous, so the example polls has_endpoint() with a three-second deadline. Losing the responder can fail an in-flight call with responder_gone.

docs.title: Transport boundaries
docs.text:
The reviewed endpoint API also declares streaming and fire-and-forget methods. The runnable endpoint example validates request/reply only; the RPC example validates all three worker RPC modes.

In-process duplicate endpoint registration is tested to raise already_hosted. The tested gRPC build accepted a second registration from the same attach and replaced the host, despite the default takeover=False. Do not rely on duplicate-registration rejection being identical across transports. Endpoint enumeration also exposes different detail in-process and over gRPC.

For Entry routing, run the Scaling harness with --tools and a runner built with both loadable and python-source-plugin. It deploys the source plugin, calls echo.describe() through Entry, hosts the application endpoint through the same backend attach, and receives the worker's result. Backend tokens belong on the trusted admin connection; the join ticket belongs to the media member.

docs.title: Cleanup and limits
docs.text:
Close streams, endpoint hosts, attaches, and finally the owned session. The MS2 supervisor also checks descendant process exit. Some native worker shutdowns log a copy-accounting closure error even when all children exit; see troubleshooting. Process cleanup and complete copy-accounting records are separate claims.

docs.title: Join Scaling with Python WebRTC
docs.text: Python applications can deploy a pipeline through Entry HTTP, obtain a member admission ticket, and negotiate WebRTC with the selected runner. The Python control package supplies the backend gRPC attach; the example uses HTTP, WebSocket signaling, and aiortc for the other boundaries.

docs.title: Prepare the media client
docs.text:
Use the media profile with the matching checkout client, aiortc==1.14.0, av==16.1.0, and websockets==15.0.1. Keep run.py and media_client.py together. You also need the echo manifest, and Entry/runner binaries identified by your runtime build.

python examples/scaling/run.py --media --bin-dir C:/path/to/scaling/debug

This creates and deletes a new local test pipeline and session. It opens no microphone or speaker. Ports and names are generated for each run, and all waits are bounded. Run --tools separately when validating the worker RPC and application endpoint graph.

docs.title: Follow the admission flow
docs.text:
1. The harness generates an ephemeral signing key and writes only its public key for Entry. Short-lived backend and client JWTs remain in memory.
  2. A backend token authorizes PUT /pipelines/{name} on the admin listener.
  3. A client token scoped to pipeline, session and member authorizes POST /join on the public listener.
  4. The client connects to the returned signal_url and sends peer.announce with the ticket. It uses the admitted peer_id returned by the runner.
  5. The client adds an audio track, creates the data channel, gathers candidates, and sends peer.offer to remotemedia-server. It applies the answer and subsequent peer.ice_candidate notifications.
  6. The client sends a 440 Hz tone and receives echoed audio. Finally it closes tracks, tasks, socket and peer connection; the harness deletes the session and pipeline and stops its owned servers.

Treat tickets as credentials. The report retains no private signing key, JWT or join ticket. For an existing service, follow its TLS, ICE/STUN/TURN and authorization configuration; this host-interface test does not establish internet or NAT traversal.

docs.title: Match the room's output stream
docs.text:
The graph is echo: PassThrough → audio: FastResampleNode. The resampler is configured with target_rate: 48000 and output_stream_id: default. Incoming room audio carries the participant's stream ID; a plain echo preserves it. The tested room's outgoing audio track is named default, so the graph must map the output to that name. Without the mapping, the runner logged that no track matched and dropped the samples.

The client adds audio before creating its data channel when using RTCBundlePolicy.MAX_BUNDLE. Reversing that order with the pinned aiortc version left this test's ICE state at new. Keep the tested order and consume candidate notifications throughout the connection. See the official aiortc API for the peer connection and media track contracts.

docs.title: What the check establishes
docs.text:
The recorded local run reaches connection: connected, data_channel: open, and receives 20 decoded 48 kHz audio frames with nonzero RMS and a spectral peak at 440 Hz. It verifies authentication rejection without a backend token and confirms owned server processes stop. It does not measure perceived quality, device latency, sustained operation, packet-loss resilience, or a remote physical network.

Inspect the generated result.json, entry.log, and runner.log beneath the selected output directory. A successful join alone does not establish successful ICE, codec negotiation, or media delivery.

docs.title: Observe and change a running session
docs.text: Attach to a live session to inspect traffic and control individual nodes. Addresses identify a node, direction, and optional port: source.in, source.out, or source.in.context.

docs.title: Run the control example
docs.text:
With the MS2 native profile:

python examples/python/session_control.py

The complete example creates source → sink, subscribes before publishing, and checks the downstream result after every decision. Its executed scope is in-process control. Remote control and Entry have separate setup and transport limits.

Operation Effect await ctrl.subscribe("source.out") Observe original output before an interceptor rewrites it await ctrl.subscribe_in("source.in") Observe live input await ctrl.publish("source.in", data) Enqueue input for processing await ctrl.publish_out("source.out.external", data) Publish to control-bus output subscribers; does not run the downstream graph ctrl.intercept("source.out", deadline_ms=...) Receive an output decision request await request.replace(Data.from_text(...)) Replace the value delivered downstream await request.drop() / pass_through() Discard or forward that output

An input publication acknowledgement is not a processing result. Wait for the downstream event, application completion marker, or RPC reply you need. Taps are live observation channels, not durable replay logs. Subscribe first and close each iterator with aclose() when leaving early.

docs.title: Set an interception deadline
docs.text:
An excerpt for an already attached control client:

import asyncio
from remotemedia.control import Data

async def replace_one(ctrl):
    async with ctrl.intercept("source.out", deadline_ms=2000) as decisions:
        await ctrl.publish("source.in", "original")
        decision = await asyncio.wait_for(anext(decisions), 5)
        await decision.replace(Data.from_text("rewritten"))

The example uses a long decision window for a tutorial; the API's default is 50 ms. The reviewed runtime forwards the original value when a decision expires. Keep slow network or model work out of a short interception window. Inspect the sink to verify a replacement: an output tap on source still sees the original.

docs.title: Override node state
docs.text: NodeState.DISABLED stops normal processing; BYPASS forwards input without running the node; ENABLED requests normal processing. await ctrl.clear_node_state("source") removes the override. The example verifies no disabled output during a 200 ms window, then verifies bypass and reset with distinct inputs. This observation is not a universal queue-flush or timing guarantee.

docs.title: Carry identity deliberately
docs.text:
The checkout accepts metadata={"request_id": "docs-1"} on publication. The tested in-process input tap returns empty metadata for that value; the example records this limitation instead of asserting preservation. Do not use this path as proof of end-to-end identity propagation.

For participant identity, the shared-session example checks the participant attached to recv_event() outputs. In Scaling, the admitted member is bound to its ticket. Treat application correlation metadata and authenticated participant identity as different fields.

docs.title: Share a session and model resources
docs.text:
Sharing a pipeline session, choosing node instance scope, and reusing a model in a worker solve different problems. Keep conversation and participant state separate from reusable model weights.

Scope What is shared What to keep separate Shared FFI session One running graph addressed by a shared session key Participant ID, role, track and modality Node instance_scope One node for the session, or one instance per participant Per-speaker accumulation and histories when using per_participant Shared Python worker/model Compatible model resource and process Each attached session's node instance and mutable conversation state Scaling room Runner-hosted session with admitted members Member identity and lifecycle under Entry

docs.title: Join and leave a local session
docs.text:
Using the MS2 native profile:

python examples/python/shared_session.py

The complete example opens Alice and Bob with the same unique shared_session_key and manifest. Both receive attributed events from the same session. Alice leaves; Bob continues. After Bob leaves, a new join under the same key creates a new session ID. Every handle is closed in finally.

The native entry point accepts a manifest JSON string, shared session key, participant ID and role, with optional track ID, modality and display name. Read outputs with recv_event() to retain the participant field alongside kind and data. A receive strategy consumes queues: do not also drain those same outputs with recv_output() in another task.

docs.title: Choose node instance scope
docs.text: The manifest's node-level instance_scope can be shared or per_participant; a node can also declare a default. Choose per-participant state for a speech buffer or speaker-specific history. Choose shared state when participants intentionally interact through one conversation component. A participant handle alone does not make every node private.

docs.title: Reuse a model safely
docs.text:
Python nodes can declare @shareable(key=("model", "device")) and acquire a resource with self.shared_resource(key, factory, on_switch=...). The sharing key should include every parameter that changes model compatibility. Voice choice or per-session history need not be part of a model key when the model supports those controls per call.

The returned handle owns access and release, and serializes model calls by default. Use the handle as a synchronous context manager on its own executor when model work would block the event loop. on_switch is where a stateful model can reset internal caches between sessions. Outside a shared worker, each handle owns a private resource.

These model-sharing semantics were checked with the captured SDK's 15 shared-resource tests and its real IPC shared-worker test: two sessions maintained independent counters, loaded one model, survived one session leaving, and shut down with exit code zero. This is separate evidence from the FFI participant example; it does not establish multi-machine model deduplication or device performance.

docs.title: Scaling room ownership
docs.text: The reviewed Scaling room host persists until Entry ends its partition. Do not apply the local FFI example's last-member teardown rule to a Scaling room. The deploy/join harness explicitly deletes the session and pipeline, then stops only its owned local servers.

docs.title: Package a Python source plugin
docs.text: A Python source plugin packages importable node code and dependency declarations behind plugin.toml. The runtime resolves the plugin, imports its entry module in a worker, and registers its declared node types. It does not require a Rust dynamic library.

docs.title: Prepare the plugin directory
docs.text:
The runnable example has two files:

examples/plugins/docs_transform/
  plugin.toml
  docs_transform.py

Download the manifest and node module. The manifest is complete:

[plugin]
name = "docs-transform"
version = "0.1.0"
language = "python"
description = "A configured text transform loaded from Python source"
license = "MIT"

[python]
entry_module = "docs_transform"
node_types = ["DocsSourceTransform"]
requires = ["packaging==25.0"]
module_root = "."

entry_module is an import name, module_root is relative to the plugin directory, and node_types identifies registered names. requires contains Python dependency requirements; this fixture pins packaging==25.0 and actually imports it. Pin the dependencies and model assets that determine your production behavior; one pinned direct dependency does not freeze the full environment.

The constructor requires NodeConfig, reads the configured prefix, and rejects a bare node ID. initialize() acquires resources, process() returns a RuntimeData text value, and cleanup() releases resources when the node owns any. Register the class under the same node type named in the manifest.

docs.title: Load it through a manifest
docs.text:
Use the MS2 native profile, a working uv installation on PATH, and the matching Python client source. This PowerShell excerpt selects that client for managed environments:

$env:REMOTEMEDIA_PYTHON_SRC = (Resolve-Path ../remotemedia-sdk/clients/python).Path
python examples/python/source_plugin.py

The complete launcher places the absolute directory path in the pipeline's plugins list, sets __python_version__ to 3.12, requests prefix SOURCE:, and waits up to 120 seconds for creation. Managed provisioning can take longer on a cold machine; the validation supervisor has a separate process deadline. The fixture checks SOURCE: HELLO, a distinct worker PID, and the installed dependency version.

The recorded run resolved a managed environment under the Windows user's .config/remotemedia/envs cache. The source loader passes the plugin dependency list, module search path, entry module and plugin identity into the worker environment. This path needs plugin resolution (loadable) and the native python-source-plugin feature. The earlier MS1 wheel and runner did not include it.

python_env.explicit_venv selects an already prepared environment instead of demonstrating managed provisioning. Use that deliberately for controlled environments; do not claim requires was provisioned merely because an explicit environment already contains its packages.

docs.title: Package and publish deliberately
docs.text:
Ship the manifest and every imported module beneath the declared module root. Local directory loading is the executed fixture. The resolver also supports remote plugin specifications; a remote tag/archive publication and verification gate is a separate task. Check the staged files and the actual release archive before claiming a published package is complete.

remotemedia.runtime.load_plugin(...) is the native shared-library loader in the reviewed build. Do not pass this Python directory to it; use the pipeline plugins field.

docs.title: Cleanup and deployment
docs.text:
The launcher closes the session in finally; the supervisor records child exit and fails if it must kill remaining children. Environment caches are reusable artifacts and are not removed as session cleanup. Avoid deleting a cache while another worker holds it.

For Entry-routed tools, the local Scaling harness uses this directory on the runner's filesystem. A distributed deployment must make the same package and compatible environment available on each eligible runner; a local absolute path is not a remote upload.

docs.title: Stream inputs and outputs
docs.text: Create a streaming session when input arrives over time or one input produces several outputs. The application owns the session and closes it when finished.

docs.title: Run the example
docs.text:
After installation, run:

python examples/python/streaming_echo.py

The complete example reads the echo manifest, sends two text inputs concurrently with receiving, signals completion, and closes in finally. Use the local environment's Python. It verifies the graph's two expected echoes: data hello and data again.

"""Send two inputs, receive their two echoes across output kinds, and close.

This graph has a known one-output-per-input contract. Input completion alone
does not establish that the installed runtime will close every output channel.
"""

import asyncio
from pathlib import Path

import remotemedia.runtime as rt


async def send_inputs(session):
    for text in ("hello", "again"):
        await session.send_input(text)
    await session.signal_input_complete()


async def receive_outputs(session):
    received = []
    for _ in range(2):
        output = await session.recv_output()
        if output is None:
            raise RuntimeError("Echo session ended before both outputs arrived")
        kind, data = output
        print(kind, data)
        received.append((kind, data))
    assert received == [("data", "hello"), ("data", "again")]


async def exchange(session):
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tasks:
        tasks.create_task(send_inputs(session))
        tasks.create_task(receive_outputs(session))


async def main():
    manifest = Path(__file__).with_name("echo.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    session = await asyncio.wait_for(rt.create_streaming_session(manifest), timeout=10)
    try:
        await asyncio.wait_for(exchange(session), timeout=10)
    finally:
        await session.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Receive every output kind
docs.text:
The native surface takes a JSON manifest string:

import remotemedia.runtime as rt

async def echo_stream(manifest_json):
    session = await rt.create_streaming_session(manifest_json)
    try:
        await session.send_input("hello")
        await session.signal_input_complete()
        output = await session.recv_output()
        if output is None:
            raise RuntimeError("Echo session ended without its expected output")
        kind, data = output
        print(kind, data)
    finally:
        await session.close()

This short example sends one item. For sustained input, use the producer/consumer structure in the complete example so an output queue cannot block a producer that is waiting to finish all its sends.

recv_output() returns (kind, data), with kind equal to audio, video, or data; it returns None after all output-kind channels close. The kind-specific methods are recv_audio(), recv_video(), and recv_data(). Choose one consumption strategy; competing readers consume from the same queues.

docs.title: Complete and close
docs.text:
signal_input_complete() closes input while allowing output to drain. Later send_input() calls fail. close() tears down the session and is idempotent. Closing immediately after the last send can discard output you intended to receive, so consume the expected results first for finite work.

In the tested local profile, both echoes arrive but input completion alone does not produce observed EOF. The initial ten-second drain check timed out; the repeat lifecycle probe also timed out. Explicit close() followed by recv_output() returns None. The example uses the echo graph's known output count. For variable-output graphs, define an application completion event or stop condition and verify it on the deployed runtime.

Boundary checked Observed result Send after input completion RuntimeError: input channel closed Timeout awaiting an empty output queue TimeoutError; explicit close succeeds Consumer exits with unread output Close succeeds; unread output is discarded Close twice Both calls succeed Receive after close None

Run python scripts/verify_examples.py to repeat these checks. Each fresh process must exit without forced child cleanup. After a cancelled receive, close the session; resuming consumption after that cancellation is unverified. close() may wait on receiver locks, so cancel/finish application receive tasks before closing.

A graph with an ongoing source may not finish simply because external input ended. Use an application deadline or stop condition and close the session. Cancelling generation inside a node is a separate operation from ending session input.

docs.title: Attribute and inspect output
docs.text:
recv_event() returns output with participant information. create_shared_streaming_session() lets local participants join a shared key; each handle leaves on close, and the last handle shuts the shared session down. Dedicated shared-session examples are planned.

Session input_copy_report() and node_copy_reports() expose different accounting scopes. Buffer policies and reports need their own guide; their presence does not establish zero-copy across an entire graph or network.

Continue with session control to inspect a specific node or inject data at a named input.

docs.title: MS2 runtime observations
docs.text:
These observations apply to the named MS2 profiles; they do not establish behavior for every release.

Symptom Reproduced cause and action Strict audio input raises BufferError A Python list requires materialization. Supply a compatible buffer and inspect the rejected-copy reason. An audio output cannot be mutated The native export is a read-only memoryview. Keep its owner or make an explicit writable NumPy copy. Input tap loses request_id metadata The tested in-process path produced empty tap metadata. Use attributed events for participant identity and verify your metadata boundary. publish_out() does not run the next node It delivers to control-bus subscribers. Publish to an input to enqueue graph work. RPC stream has no aclose() Close aiter(ctrl.node.method(...)), not the deferred call object. RPC named status() raises NodeStatus is not callable The name shadows a worker instance attribute. Choose a distinct name such as generation_state. gRPC endpoint still appears immediately after close Remote unhosting is asynchronous. Poll with a deadline; the example allows three seconds. Duplicate endpoint registration differs over gRPC The tested gRPC same-attach registration replaced the old host; in-process registration rejected it. Do not assume duplicate rejection parity. Source plugin fails on join The runner needs both loadable and python-source-plugin. Missing either produced a join error in the test builds. WebRTC ICE stays new with aiortc 1.14.0 and MAX_BUNDLE Creating the data channel before audio caused this test's stall. Follow the tested audio-first setup. WebRTC connects but receives no echoed audio The runner dropped an unmatched participant stream ID. Map it to the room's default audio track with FastResampleNode.output_stream_id. Python copy accounting did not close cleanly on worker shutdown Some tested native shutdowns report incomplete accounting closure despite successful outputs and no surviving children. Retain the diagnostic; process exit does not establish accounting conservation. No runtime fix is claimed here.

The data, session control, RPC/tools, cancellation, and media examples retain these boundaries explicitly.

Run python examples/python/doctor.py --require-ffi with the same interpreter as the failing local example. For remote control, omit --require-ffi. Keep the imported paths and versions with the failure report.

docs.title: Native module is missing
docs.text:
No module named 'remotemedia.runtime' means the client environment cannot import FFI. Install a compatible native wheel into that exact environment. The diagnostic explains this and exits unsuccessfully when FFI is required. A remote-only control environment is expected to work without FFI.

If Windows reports a DLL load error, record the wheel filename, architecture, native path, and dependency error. A package version match alone does not verify binary dependencies. Follow the tested install profile.

docs.title: Package installation attempts a native build
docs.text: For the tested Windows/Python combination, PyPI has no usable binary wheel for FFI 0.4.4. A normal install falls back to its source distribution. Use a supplied compatible wheel for this guide; a Rust source build needs its own toolchain and validation. Do not substitute an arbitrary cached binary without recording its identity.

docs.title: Attach rejects the token keyword
docs.text:
TypeError mentioning an unexpected token argument indicates an older client API. The published remotemedia-client==0.2.0 lacks it, while the reviewed checkout (also version 0.2.0) includes it. Use the separate checkout control environment.

For 401/403 from Entry, check token role, expiry, developer public key, and listener. Backend control requires a backend token and the admin address. Client admission requires the client token and public /join endpoint.

docs.title: Deployment returns 422
docs.text: Read the response's problems list. The local harness initially reproduced a mismatch between the URL pipeline name and manifest.metadata.name; making them equal allowed deployment. The harness retains server error details without printing authorization headers.

docs.title: Echo arrived but the stream never ends
docs.text: Input completion and output EOF are distinct. The tested native wheel delivered both echoes but did not close every channel after signal_input_complete(). Stop on the graph's expected result count or explicit application completion signal, cancel/finish receive tasks, and await session.close() in finally. Do not use an unbounded drain loop for this artifact. See streaming lifecycle.

docs.title: A tap receives no output
docs.text: Subscribe before publishing, use the correct .out address and node ID, and verify input reaches the live session. An expired wait on an otherwise idle tap does not establish a broken session. Taps observe new output and do not replay history.

docs.title: Worker IPC does not initialize
docs.text:
Without access to the host's IPC paths, the Windows worker attempt failed with:

Failed to create global iceoryx2 node: InternalError
create_session failed: ... IPC error: Node not initialized

This failure happens before the custom node initializes. Check the host's iceoryx2 IPC filesystem permissions and compatibility between the native build and Python iceoryx2 package. This host uses C:\Temp\, C:\Temp\iceoryx2\, and C:\Temp\iceoryx2\shm\; workspace-only write access was insufficient. Authorized access resolved initialization. Do not delete shared IPC files belonging to other sessions.

The example selects an explicit virtual environment and importable on-disk module. Rerun .venv-worker/Scripts/python.exe scripts/verify_examples.py --worker and require transformed output, the RPC-reported worker PID, configuration preservation, and normal process-tree exit. All these checks passed with the worker profile.

docs.title: Dotted node type is not registered
docs.text: Node type 'node_transform.DocsUppercase' not registered was reproduced with the published client after IPC access was enabled. The current registry supports importing dotted class paths. Use the checkout client and matching Python native wheel, keep the module directory importable in the worker, and select that environment with python_env.explicit_venv.

docs.title: Worker transforms text but RPC times out
docs.text:
The worker can return a reply tagged with the rpc text-channel header. A reply reader that parses the whole tagged string as JSON silently ignores it. The checked-in client fix strips that header before decoding; regression tests cover tagged and untagged replies. Install the checkout including this fix, then rerun the complete worker verifier. A longer timeout cannot repair this decoding error.
